trivia: On my smaller island, the land has belonged to the islanders in common ever since emancipation in 1834. A 2007 law says none of it can be sold and every islander can claim plots for a home, a farm and a business, though a 2017 change by the national government is still bitterly contested.

trivia: In 1998 Eric Clapton, sober since 1987, opened Crossroads, a 36-bed addiction-treatment centre on my main island. He funds it partly through his Crossroads Guitar Festival, and some beds are set aside for local people who can't pay.

My uninhabited rock island of Redonda, about a mile long, has more kings than people. Since a writer claimed it as a 'kingdom' in the 1800s, a string of novelists and poets have called themselves King of Redonda, handing out titles like 'Duke of Guano' to their literary friends.

trivia: My national dress, chosen in a 1992 design competition won by artist Heather Doram, copies what market vendors and bakers wore in 1834, the year of emancipation: a red, gold and green madras-plaid dress with a crisp white pinafore and headscarf.

trivia: My Carnival, first held in 1957, celebrates the end of slavery on 1 August 1834. It peaks with J'ouvert, from the French for 'daybreak': revellers covered in paint and mud dance through St John's from before dawn until mid-morning.

trivia: My national dish is fungee and pepperpot: fungee is cornmeal stirred with okra into a smooth, polenta-like ball, and pepperpot is a thick stew of salted meat, aubergine and greens ladled around it.

trivia: My national fruit is a small 'black' pineapple, which isn't black at all. Often called the sweetest in the world, it is so soft and delicate that it can hardly be exported, and it even appears on my coat of arms.
My favourite side dish is ducana: grated sweet potato and coconut, sweetened and spiced, wrapped in a banana leaf and boiled into a dumpling. It is eaten with saltfish, dried and salted cod.

trivia: The highest individual score in Test cricket history, Brian Lara's 400 not out against England in 2004, was made at the Recreation Ground in St John's. Ten years earlier, on the very same ground and against the same team, he had set the old record of 375.

trivia: In Codrington Lagoon on my smaller island lives the Caribbean's largest colony of magnificent frigatebirds, more than 5,000 birds. In the breeding season the males inflate huge red throat pouches like balloons to attract females.

trivia: In 1995 my harmless grey-brown racer snake was the rarest snake on Earth: just 50 survived, on Great Bird Island, many bitten by rats. After conservationists cleared the rats and moved snakes to Rabbit, Green and York islands, there are now more than 1,100.

trivia: My proud claim is 365 beaches, one for every day of the year, squeezed around an island of just 108 square miles. All of them are open to the public.
My flat smaller island is fringed by 17 Mile Beach, said to be the longest unbroken beach in the Caribbean, and by sand tinted pink by crushed coral and shells.

trivia: In September 2017 Hurricane Irma, a Category 5 storm whose eye was big enough to swallow my whole smaller island, damaged or destroyed about 95% of its buildings. All 1,800 residents were evacuated, and for the first time in over 300 years, nobody lived there.

Nelson's Dockyard in English Harbour is the only Georgian-era naval dockyard in the world still working today, and a UNESCO site since 2016. Yet young Horatio Nelson, stationed there in the 1780s, called the place an 'infernal hole'.

In 1685 King Charles II leased my whole smaller island to the Codrington brothers. The rent: 'one fat sheep yearly, if demanded'. The family kept it for almost two centuries, and its only village is still called Codrington.

When Britain abolished slavery in 1834, most colonies forced the freed people to keep working for their old masters as 'apprentices' for four more years. My planters' assembly chose immediate, full freedom instead, one of only two colonies to do so, alongside Bermuda.

My tiny island of Redonda was once a busy mine for guano, centuries of seabird droppings used as fertiliser. About 200 workers lived there in 1901, shipping up to 7,000 tons a year to the US and Germany, until the First World War cut off the trade and the island was abandoned for good.

trivia: Since 2013 you can buy my passport: a donation of at least US$230,000 to my National Development Fund gets a family of four citizenship, and they only need to spend 5 days here in the first 5 years.

trivia: Texan financier Allen Stanford became my largest employer, was knighted here in 2006 and poured millions into a cricket tournament watched by 300 million. In 2012 he was jailed for 110 years: his offshore bank in St John's had been a $7 billion Ponzi scheme, and I stripped him of his knighthood.
